candidate_matrix_revisions.effect: Confirms the mechanism identified locally in H-20260923-09 (return autocorrelation, not diversification, drove S3's return) generalizes across leveraged ETFs, so candidate lanes were restricted to industries with an independent, currently-trending narrative (gold miners, regional banks, aerospace/defense) rather than scanned across all levered ETFs.

Gives a decades-old, independently replicated mechanism (industry return continuation) as the economic reason a second sector lane could work, so the five lanes are grounded in the Ken French top-ranked recent industries (I-20260923-01) rather than being a backtest-fit ETF pick.

Formalizes that multi-day holding return is not N times the index's multi-day return; the spec's notes and the eventual report must carry the daily-reset caveat explicitly for every lane, not only for the already-live S3 book.

The vt40+boost overlay machine is reused byte-for-byte from the live S3 renewal rather than re-searched, so this round tests exactly one new thing (which lane) instead of re-opening the overlay's own parameters.

Keeps the 2026 holdout strictly scored-once and never used to rank, and requires both the pool-rank and calendar-shift placebos (G3) before any lane can be treated as a real pass rather than an in-sample artifact.

objective: Ask whether a second levered sector lane, beyond semiconductors, clears the frozen S3-machine gates and is weakly correlated with the live S3 book, using published industry-momentum evidence and the local giants-sweep/attribution record to pick the five candidates instead of scanning the full levered-ETF universe.

sources.core_claim: Moreira and Muir show that scaling factor exposure down when realized volatility is high raises Sharpe ratios for the market, value, momentum, profitability, return-on-equity and investment factors and for the currency carry trade, because factor volatility changes are not offset by proportional changes in expected returns.
sources.project_applicability: The live S3 vt40+boost overlay this round reuses unchanged is a direct application of this mechanism to a levered-ETF sleeve; the second-bet lanes inherit the same frozen overlay, so this evidence still grounds why the overlay itself is trustworthy even though this round's actual question is which lane to run it on.
sources.reflection: Long-short factor portfolios with unconstrained leverage, monthly data, no transaction costs, sample ends a decade before our anchor window.

sources.core_claim: Across 103 equity strategies, volatility-managed portfolios do not systematically beat their unmanaged counterparts for a real-time investor: the spanning-regression alphas are not implementable and out-of-sample versions generally earn lower certainty equivalents and Sharpe ratios than simply holding the unmanaged portfolio.
sources.project_applicability: Keeps this round honest about the overlay: the 2026 holdout is scored once and never used to pick a lane, and G2/G4 stay pass/fail gates rather than in-sample flattery.
sources.reflection: Monthly long-short equity factors, real-time estimation of the scaling coefficient; it does not test a fixed target-volatility rule with a hard leverage cap on a levered-ETF sleeve.

sources.core_claim: After transaction costs, volatility management of asset-pricing factors other than the market generally produces zero abnormal returns and significantly lower Sharpe ratios, while the volatility-managed market portfolio stays robust to costs.
sources.project_applicability: Reused reason G4 (20 bp stress) stays a hard gate rather than a footnote for every lane, not just for S3 itself.
sources.reflection: Factor portfolios, not ETFs; cost model is US equity spreads, not ETF spreads.

sources.core_claim: Across more than 60 assets with daily data from 1926, volatility scaling raises Sharpe ratios for risk assets (equities and credit) and for portfolios with a large allocation to them, and consistently reduces the likelihood of extreme returns.
sources.project_applicability: General support for applying the same frozen overlay to a new equity-beta lane, independent of which industry it is.
sources.reflection: Practitioner research by a manager that sells volatility-targeted products; unlevered assets, no ETF path-dependency or borrow costs.

sources.core_claim: In 45 international equity markets, only the volatility-managed market and momentum strategies are partially robust to transaction costs, suggesting most of the abnormal return of volatility management is explained by costs.
sources.project_applicability: Keeps the prior that the overlay's edge is cost-marginal in general, so this round's actual edge (if any) must come from the lane's own trend, not from the overlay.
sources.reflection: International factor portfolios; no levered ETF or daily-rebalanced sleeve.

sources.core_claim: Quantpedia proposes gating leveraged-ETF exposure with a volatility filter that compares short-term realized volatility with implied volatility, cutting exposure in high-volatility periods to keep the leverage while mitigating the worst drawdowns.
sources.project_applicability: Closest published analogue of the frozen overlay on the exact instrument class (leveraged sector ETFs), independent of which sector.
sources.reflection: Vendor blog, rules described but thresholds not fully public, no live track record, uses an implied-volatility input we do not have PIT.

sources.core_claim: Leveraged ETFs do not work in long-term passive portfolios because they amplify losses and volatility, but simple trend filters (10-month moving average, 12-month high) reduce the damage when leverage is actively managed.
sources.project_applicability: Independent confirmation that an active risk overlay, not buy-and-hold, is the only defensible way to run any single levered sector ETF, including the five new lanes.
sources.reflection: Vendor blog, monthly trend rules only, no cost or capacity analysis of our sleeve.

sources.core_claim: Open-loop volatility targeting that scales exposure inversely with a variance forecast suffers from high turnover, leverage spikes and sensitivity to estimation error; a proportional-control formulation hits the target volatility more consistently.
sources.project_applicability: Same reason the frozen machine keeps a monthly overlay update and a hard 1.0 leverage cap for every lane rather than a daily inverse-variance scaler.
sources.reflection: Simulation only, no live or historical trading record, not peer reviewed.

sources.core_claim: Kenneth French's 49 Industry Portfolios dataset assigns each NYSE, AMEX, and NASDAQ stock to one of 49 industry portfolios at the end of June of year t using its four-digit SIC code at that time, then computes returns from July of t to June of t+1, with daily, monthly, and annual return files spanning July 1926 to the present.
sources.project_applicability: This is the provider-official methodology behind the local I-20260923-01 census that ranked Gold, Chips, Banks and Aero as the top four select-window industries and motivated this round's five candidate lanes (gold miners and financials/banks; chips is already the live S3 book).
sources.reflection: Describes construction only, not the I-20260923-01 return numbers themselves (a local first-party computation); industries are unlevered cap-weighted baskets, not the specific leveraged ETFs this round tests.

sources.core_claim: Moskowitz and Grinblatt (1999, Journal of Finance) document a strong and prevalent momentum effect in industry components of stock returns that accounts for much of the individual-stock momentum anomaly: industry momentum strategies that buy past winning industries and sell past losing industries are highly profitable even after controlling for size, book-to-market, individual stock momentum, cross-sectional dispersion in mean returns, and microstructure effects.
sources.project_applicability: The economic mechanism behind the whole direction: a second trending industry is a documented, decades-replicated effect, not an ad hoc ETF pick, which is why the five candidates were chosen from Ken French's top-ranked recent industries rather than by scanning all levered ETFs for the best backtest.
sources.reflection: Unlevered, monthly-rebalanced industry portfolios with no transaction costs modeled at the ETF-spread level; a 1963-1995 sample that predates our 2023-2026 windows and says nothing about leverage, daily reset, or volatility targeting.

sources.core_claim: Hsieh et al. (arXiv 2504.20116) show that leveraged ETF performance depends fundamentally on return autocorrelation and return dynamics rather than only volatility drag: in markets with independent returns LETFs exhibit positive expected compounding on their target multiple, serially correlated (trending) markets enhance daily-rebalanced LETF returns, and mean-reverting regimes cause underperformance.
sources.project_applicability: Directly explains the mechanism behind the live S3 book found in H-20260923-09 (116.3% anchor return concentrated in SOXL+USD, 58.5% anchor / 69.4% holdout average weight) and is the reason this round looks for a second industry with an independent trend driver rather than assuming any leveraged sector ETF would compound favorably.
sources.reflection: Theoretical/simulation paper with an empirical section limited to SPY and QQQ, not to any of the five candidate 2x/3x sector ETFs; a preprint, not yet peer reviewed.

sources.core_claim: Direxion's DPST (Daily Regional Banks Bull 3X ETF) seeks a return of 300% of its benchmark index for a single day only; the fund should not be expected to provide three times the benchmark's cumulative return for periods greater than a day.
sources.project_applicability: LN04 (DPST) daily-reset disclosure; the spec's notes must carry forward that the machine's 63-session momentum and monthly rebalance operate on a path that compounds daily 3x exposure, not a fixed 3x multiple of any multi-day return.
sources.reflection: Marketing/product page, not a prospectus; no historical compounding-decay magnitude or financing-cost detail.

sources.core_claim: Direxion's NUGT and DUST (Daily Gold Miners Index Bull and Bear 2X ETFs) seek a return of 200% or -200% of their benchmark index for a single day only; the funds should not be expected to provide two times or negative two times the benchmark's cumulative return for periods greater than a day.
sources.project_applicability: LN01 (NUGT) daily-reset disclosure from a second, independent Direxion product page covering a different underlying index family (gold miners) than DPST (regional banks), confirming the caveat is issuer-wide, not fund-specific.
sources.reflection: Marketing/product page; NUGT's own since-inception NAV return is -31.53%, a reminder that a trending-regime lane can still be net-negative outside the regime it trends in, which is why this round scores lanes only on the frozen 2023-2026 windows.
